stimulus.text:
“'Twas mercy brought me from my Pagan land,
Taught my benighted soul to understand
That there's a God, that there's a Saviour too:
Once I redemption neither sought nor knew.
Some view our sable race with scornful eye,
‘Their colour is a diabolic die.’
Remember, Christians, Negroes, black as Cain,
May be refin'd, and join th' angelic train.”
— Phillis Wheatley, “On Being Brought from Africa to America,” in Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral (London, 1773)
stimulus.source_note: Phillis Wheatley, Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral (London, 1773). Public domain.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — Phillis Wheatley, “On Being Brought from Africa to America” (1773), public domain. Rewritten against the books from staged survivors 5s24-exam2-mcq-33 through -36.

books.section: Topic 3.6 The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals, A. The Call for Egalitarianism

primary_sources: Phillis Wheatley, “On Being Brought from Africa to America” (1773)

stem: Wheatley's claim that Black people “may be refin'd, and join th' angelic train” most directly anticipates the arguments of

options.text: Nineteenth-century Black abolitionists, who made Christian equality the moral core of antislavery
Southern defenders of slavery, who used the Bible to justify bondage
options.misconception: Southern defenders argued the opposite of Wheatley; they used Scripture to defend slavery, not to claim Black equality.

options.text: Deists, who rejected revealed religion as a guide to morals
options.misconception: Deists set Scripture aside; Wheatley argues inside Christianity, not against it.

options.text: Loyalist writers, who urged obedience to the king as a Christian duty
options.misconception: Loyalists argued for obedience to Britain, not for Black spiritual equality; their cause was different entirely.

rationales.A: Wheatley says Black souls share in salvation, and later Black abolitionists built their whole case on that same Christian equality. Background: Frederick Douglass and others made the Bible's equality the heart of antislavery.
rationales.B: Slaveholders cited the Bible to defend bondage, the opposite use from Wheatley's claim of shared salvation.
rationales.C: Deists rejected revelation; Wheatley leans on it, so her argument runs against deism, not with it.
rationales.D: Loyalist writers used Scripture to demand obedience, not to claim spiritual equality for Black people.
rationales.general:
1. Name her claim. Black people share in salvation, so white scorn for them offends their own faith.
2. Ask who later said the same. Background: Black abolitionists made Christian equality the heart of antislavery.
3. Check the others. Defenders of slavery, deists, and Loyalists all used Scripture differently or not at all.
Remember: an idea's future is found by asking who later needed the same argument — and used it.
